headline: Villagers in Indonesia get paid for animal photos

sources.title: A Strategy of Cash-for-Photos Turns Animal Hunters into Animal Protectors in Indonesia (Good News Network)
Indonesia cash-for-photos scheme turns animal hunters into protectors (AFP, via The Star)
Indonesia scheme turns hunters into protectors (AFP, via Taipei Times)
Indonesia's cash-for-photos scheme turns villagers into wildlife protectors (video, AFP)

chunks.text: A project in Indonesia pays villagers to photograph wild animals instead of hunting them. It runs in nine villages in the Indonesian part of the island of Borneo. Local people {{head out}} into the forest and {{send in}} photos or [[sound recordings]] of the animals they find. Many [[former hunters]] have {{turned into}} [[protectors]] of wildlife. A French news agency reported on the project on September 17, 2026.

chunks.text: An environmental [[consulting company]] called Borneo Futures {{set up}} the project in 2024. Users share each [[sighting]] through an app, and staff check that it is real. A common bird earns 5,000 rupiah, about 30 cents. An [[endangered]] orangutan earns 130,000 rupiah, the [[top prize]]. These small payments can {{add up}}. The most active observers {{bring in}} up to 10 million rupiah a month, about $570. That is several times what a typical [[farm worker]] earns.

chunks.text: Since the project began, two villages have {{given up}} hunting and [[banned]] it [[on their own]]. One 50-year-old farmer earned about $230 in September 2026. He says the photo work is a [[side job]] that {{fits in with}} his farming. One woman says the money gives her more [[independence]]. The company's director in Indonesia says one caught bird could once sell for 50,000 rupiah. Now five photos of a bird can earn the same, and the bird can still [[breed]].

mainIdea.s: Villagers in part of Indonesian Borneo now get money for photos and recordings of wild animals. Many people who once hunted help protect wildlife, but the money lasts only until 2028.
mainIdea.why: Nine villages share sightings through an app and get paid. Former hunters have turned into protectors, and the funding is set to last until 2028.

mainIdea.s: A program in Borneo pays former hunters a monthly salary to guard the forest from poachers. Every village taking part has now made hunting illegal, and the government pays the costs.
mainIdea.why: Close, but people are paid for each photo or recording, not a salary. Only two villages banned hunting, and charitable foundations put up the money.

mainIdea.s: Indonesia has opened a new national park on Borneo to protect orangutans. Officials plan to move families out of the forest and hire park rangers to stop illegal logging there.
mainIdea.why: Villagers in nine villages are paid for wildlife photos and recordings. A consulting company set up the project, and no families are being moved.

lines.text: Did you see that story about wildlife photos in Indonesia?
Villagers on Borneo {{head out}} into the forest and take photos of animals. Then they {{send in}} the pictures and get paid.
About 30 cents for a common bird. An orangutan is the top prize.
That doesn't sound like a lot.
It {{adds up}}, though. The best observers {{bring in}} about $570 a month.
Wow, that's a pretty good [[side hustle]].
And a lot of them used to be hunters. Two villages have even {{given up}} hunting.
So the hunters have {{turned into}} protectors. That's a real [[win-win]].
Right. One farmer says the photo work {{fits in with}} his farming, too.
Charitable foundations {{put up}} about $300,000. And two more villages planned to {{sign up}} in October.
What happens after the money {{runs out}}?
That's [[the million-dollar question]]. The funding only lasts until 2028.
Well, keeping a bird alive so you can photograph it again and again? That's [[a no-brainer]].
